name: Sophie Christine
headline: Making founders as known as their companies | 41M+ organic views across LinkedIn, Instagram, YouTube & newsletters

sections.bio:
You're not losing because of a lack of content.
You're losing because your audience remembers your post but forgets your name.

You post consistently.
You share good ideas.
You put in the work.

Yet six months later, you're still wondering why nobody associates you with anything specific.

I've spent years obsessing over that question.

Why do some people become known for something while others keep creating and stay invisible?
That curiosity has taken me deep into LinkedIn posts, newsletters, YouTube channels, personal brands, ad campaigns, and more internet rabbit holes than I'd like to admit.

What I've learned is that growth rarely comes from creating more.

It usually comes from making people remember you.

Over the last few years, I've helped build content strategies across LinkedIn, newsletters, Instagram, and YouTube, contributing to:

• 16M+ LinkedIn impressions
• 37K+ newsletter subscribers
• 17.8M+ YouTube views
• 200K Instagram followers

But the numbers are just evidence.

The real work happens before that.
Figuring out what a brand should be known for.
Finding the ideas worth repeating.
Turning scattered expertise into a message people can instantly understand and remember.
That's the part I enjoy most.

If you're building a brand, creator business, or audience and you're tired of creating content that gets seen but forgotten, let's talk.

posts.text:
My first freelance client came through a referral.

I was excited.

And terrified.

It was the first time someone had trusted me enough to pay for my work.

We got on a Zoom call.

For 45 minutes, he walked me through his business.
When the call ended, I thought it had gone really well.

I opened a blank document to start putting together his LinkedIn strategy.
And...

I couldn't write a single sentence.
I knew he'd explained everything.

For a moment, I thought the problem was me.
Then it hit me.

The problem was that he couldn't see his business the way an outsider would.

When you've spent years building a business, it's almost impossible to remember what it's like hearing about it for the first time.

There's actually a name for this.
The Curse of Knowledge.

It's the tendency to forget what it's like not to know what you know.

So instead of forcing a strategy, I asked if we could jump on another call.

I spent some time writing down all the questions I wished I'd asked the first time.

We went through them one by one.
I left that call with pages of notes.

This time, the strategy almost wrote itself.
The profile came together.

I'm not working with him anymore.

But that project changed how I think about positioning.

It taught me that most founders don't struggle because they have nothing to say.

They struggle because they have too much.

And when you've spent years inside your own business, it's surprisingly hard to tell what someone hearing it for the first time actually needs to know.

I was scrolling LinkedIn yesterday

and I must've read around 30 posts.

Some were genuinely useful.

I can't remember who wrote a single one.

But I can remember a creator talking about getting stuck in an airport.

That post wasn't useful.

It wasn't educational.

It didn't have a framework.

But I remember exactly who posted it.

That feels unfair.

The people putting in the most effort are often the easiest to forget.

The people I remember make me feel like I know them.

I'm starting to think "adding value" isn't enough anymore.

It's become the baseline.

People don't just remember ideas.

They remember the people attached to them.

Someone got offended because of one message I sent them.

I came across her LinkedIn profile and started reading her posts.

She had a great following and her posts were very thoughtful.

Clearly, she'd put a lot of effort into them.
So I messaged her.

"I've read quite a few of your posts, but if someone asked me what you're known for... I genuinely wouldn't know what to say."

She didn't take it well.

Her reply was:
"Did you even read my posts? I put a lot of thought into them."

And honestly, I understand why.

Because we grow up believing better writing leads to more attention.

I'm not sure that's true anymore.

There are people on LinkedIn who can post:
"My flight got delayed."
And it'll get 2,000 likes.

Not because it's a brilliant thought.

Because people already know who's talking.

Meanwhile, someone else shares genuinely useful insights...
...and nobody cares.

I think that's the shift most people miss.

People don't engage because the update is extraordinary.

They engage because they already care who's saying it.
That's why polishing every sentence isn't enough.

If people can't tell who you are after reading your content...
It doesn't matter how well you wrote it.

"I don't need a personal brand" has become a status symbol for many founders.

The problem is, too many founders have started believing it...

Usually because they benefit from one of two things:
• They built before social media changed buying behavior.
• Or people already know them because of the company they built.

If you're building today...
Staying behind your brand isn't a strategy,
it's a choice.

And every choice has a cost.
The cost isn't whether your product sells.

A great product can still sell.

The cost is the opportunities you never hear about.

When someone is looking for a founder to feature, invite, quote, or recommend...

Will your name even cross their mind?

Because your brand can be memorable.
While the person behind it stays invisible.

Being invisible is more expensive than most founders think.

I loved a product so much that I searched for the founder on LinkedIn.

I use this product regularly and genuinely like the brand, so naturally I got curious about the person who built it.

I found the founder's profile.
And there was... almost nothing.

I spent a few minutes scrolling and still couldn't tell you what they think about their own industry, why they started the company or even what they want to change through the brand.

Which felt strange because I already liked their product.

They didn't have to convince me to care. The brand had already done that.
I was literally looking for them.

And I think this is something a lot of founders underestimate.

You don't need to post every day or turn yourself into a LinkedIn creator.

But when someone likes your company enough to search your name, what do they find?
A job title?
A company name?
Three reposts from the brand page?

Because your customers can know your brand really well and still have absolutely no idea who you are.

And maybe some founders are completely fine with that.

But if you're trying to build trust, credibility or become known in your industry, you're leaving a lot on the table.

Your brand already got me to your profile.
You just gave me no reason to remember the person behind it.
